specPoints.text: understand how a nucleus of U-235 can be split (the process of fission) by collision with a neutron and that this process releases energy as kinetic energy of the fission products
know that the fission of U-235 produces two radioactive daughter nuclei and a small number of neutrons

primer.text: Uranium-235 barely decays on its own, so reactors help it along: an absorbed neutron turns it into uranium-236, which splits at once. The split leaves two radioactive daughters, two or three fresh neutrons and gamma rays, with the released energy riding out as kinetic energy of the fragments.

lessons.title: Spontaneous and induced fission
lessons.opening: A large unstable nucleus can split into two smaller nuclei, but left alone it rarely does — that rare route is spontaneous fission. Normally the nucleus first absorbs a neutron, and the added instability makes it fall apart almost at once; that is induced fission, the route reactors rely on.
keyPoints: Fission splits one big unstable nucleus into a pair of smaller nuclei.
Uranium and plutonium isotopes are fissile, so they can be reactor fuels.
Spontaneous fission is rare; induced fission starts when the nucleus absorbs a neutron.
A U-235 nucleus that absorbs a neutron becomes uranium-236, which splits almost at once.
U-235's very long half-life means its own decay releases energy far too slowly.

low.restatement: Add a neutron to U-235 and you get U-236, which splits; without the added neutron, splits almost never happen.
low.analogy: A balanced stack of plates that barely wobbles on its own — nudge it with one more plate and it topples at once.
low.examPointer: Fissile is the key adjective for uranium and plutonium isotopes; use it when explaining why they are fuels.

medium.restatement: Capture of one neutron converts U-235 into the far less stable U-236; the 700-million-year half-life explains why the spontaneous route is negligible.
medium.analogy: A lazy river that never floods until one extra tributary arrives — then the dam bursts immediately.
medium.examPointer: Do not confuse spontaneous with induced: examiners award the contrast marks only when both routes are named correctly.

check.stem: Induced fission of a uranium-235 nucleus begins when the nucleus…

options.explanation: The captured neutron makes U-236, which is highly unstable.
Alpha emission is decay, not the fission trigger.
Electrons do not induce nuclear fission.
Gamma emission changes energy, not stability enough to split.

check.stem: After absorbing a neutron, uranium-235 becomes…

options.explanation: 235 + 1 neutron = 236, and the extra mass tips it over the edge.
Absorption adds mass; it does not remove it.
U-236 is the opposite of stable — it splits at once.
Plutonium forms by other capture chains, not this one.

options.text: fission without extra energy added, and it is rare
options.explanation: Nuclei seldom split with nothing added — that is why reactors induce it.
Reactors induce fission with neutrons.
Control rods absorb neutrons; they never start splits.
It can happen, just very rarely.

check.stem: Why must reactors induce fission in uranium-235?

options.text: its 700-million-year half-life gives it low activity, so it releases energy far too slowly alone
options.explanation: The long half-life keeps spontaneous decay sluggish; neutron capture speeds things up.

options.text: because uranium is too dense to split naturally
options.explanation: Density is irrelevant to the split rate.

options.text: because reactors add protons to the nucleus
options.explanation: Neutrons, not protons, are absorbed.
It is unstable, just very slow to decay.

check.stem: Which property makes uranium and plutonium isotopes useful reactor fuels?

options.text: they are fissile — able to undergo fission under the right conditions
options.explanation: Fissile isotopes split when induced, which is exactly what fuel must do.
Fissile means reactive, not inert.
U-235's half-life is 700 million years — long, not short.
They capture neutrons — that is the point.

check.stem: State what must be absorbed to induce fission in uranium-235.
check.modelAnswer: A neutron must be absorbed; the nucleus becomes uranium-236 and splits almost immediately.
Spontaneous fission is fission that happens without extra energy being put in, and it is rare.

check.stem: Explain why uranium-235's long half-life makes induced fission necessary in power stations.
check.modelAnswer: A 700-million-year half-life means very low activity, so uranium-235 trickles out energy far too slowly to run a station; absorbing a neutron builds the much less stable uranium-236, which splits straight away and delivers useful power.

check.stem: A neutron strikes a uranium-235 nucleus. Name the isotope formed and state what it does next.
check.modelAnswer: The nucleus becomes uranium-236, which is so unstable that it splits by fission almost immediately.

lessons.title: Products and energy of fission
lessons.opening: When induced fission splits a uranium-235 nucleus, the products are two radioactive daughter nuclei, two or three neutrons, and gamma rays — barium-144 and krypton-89 are one real pair. The daughters and neutrons fly apart fast because nuclear potential energy has become their kinetic energy, and power stations convert that into electrical energy.
keyPoints: Induced fission of U-235 produces two radioactive daughters, two or three neutrons, and gamma rays.
One actual split of U-235 makes barium-144 and krypton-89.
Energy stored as nuclear potential energy becomes kinetic energy of the fast products.
Nuclear power stations convert that kinetic energy into electrical energy.

low.restatement: One split: two radioactive daughters, two-to-three neutrons, gamma rays; the stored nuclear energy becomes their motion.
low.analogy: A wound-up spring toy snaps open: the stored tension (potential energy) turns into the pieces flying across the floor (kinetic energy).
low.examPointer: Balance fission equations exactly like decay equations — subtract products from the parent to find the missing piece.

medium.restatement: Product census per fission: 2 daughters + 2–3 neutrons + gamma rays; energy conservation moves nuclear potential energy into product kinetic energy.
medium.analogy: A plant pot cracking into two shards that skid across the patio — the crack releases the stress that was stored in the clay.
medium.examPointer: Daughters' names are not required in exams — balancing the numbers is; practise the subtraction method on plutonium and uranium cases.

check.stem: Which set correctly lists the products of one U-235 fission?

options.text: two radioactive daughter nuclei and two or three neutrons
options.explanation: That is the standard product pair-plus-neutrons census.

options.text: one daughter nucleus and one neutron
options.explanation: Two daughters and at least two neutrons emerge.

options.text: three daughter nuclei and no neutrons
options.explanation: Neutrons always accompany the split.

options.text: two stable daughters with nothing else emitted
options.explanation: The daughters are radioactive and gamma rays also emerge.

check.stem: Alongside daughters and neutrons, the fission also emits…

options.explanation: Gamma emission accompanies the split.

options.text: alpha particles as the main emission
options.explanation: Alphas are not the listed fission emission.
Protons stay bound in the daughters.
Gamma rays are emitted too.

check.stem: The fission fragments shoot apart very quickly because…

options.text: nuclear potential energy has been transferred to their kinetic energy
options.explanation: The stored nuclear energy becomes motion of the products.
The nucleus is not moved by air.
Gravity would pull them together, not shoot them apart.

options.text: the reactor core heats them up
options.explanation: The speed comes from the split itself, not core heating.

check.stem: In the example U-235 fission, the two daughters are…

options.explanation: That is the quoted daughter pair for induced fission of U-235.
The mass numbers are swapped.
Those belong to alpha decay chains.
U-236 is the pre-split nucleus, not a daughter.

check.stem: How many neutrons does a single U-235 fission release?

options.explanation: Each split releases a small number — two or three — of neutrons.
One neutron enters; more than one leaves.
That overcounts the small neutron yield.
Neutron emission is what sustains chain reactions.

check.stem: State how many daughter nuclei and neutrons one U-235 fission produces.
check.modelAnswer: Two daughter nuclei form, together with two or three neutrons.

check.stem: Name the two daughter nuclei in the example U-235 split.
Explain where the kinetic energy of the fission products comes from.
check.modelAnswer: The parent nucleus stores nuclear potential energy; when it splits, that stored energy transfers to the motion of the daughters and neutrons, which is why they fly apart at high speed.

check.stem: Plutonium-239 (mass 239, atomic 94) fissions into palladium-112 (atomic 46) and cadmium-124 (atomic 48). Work out the mass and atomic numbers of the missing products.
check.modelAnswer: Mass: 239 − (112 + 124) = 3. Atomic: 94 − (46 + 48) = 0. A particle with mass 1 and atomic 0 is a neutron, so the missing products are three neutrons.

glossary.definition: Describes isotopes, such as some of uranium and plutonium, that can undergo fission under the right conditions.
Fission started by the absorption of a neutron, making the nucleus unstable enough to split at once.
Fission that happens without extra energy added; rare in practice.
The two smaller radioactive nuclei produced when a parent nucleus splits.

workedExample.prompt: During a spontaneous fission reaction, plutonium-239 splits into palladium-112 and cadmium-124. What is emitted to balance the equation?
steps: Mass numbers: 239 − (112 + 124) = 3, so the missing mass number is 3.
Atomic numbers: 94 − (46 + 48) = 0, so the missing atomic number is 0.
A particle with mass number 1 and atomic number 0 is a neutron, and three of them give mass 3 with atomic 0.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Three neutrons (total mass number 3, atomic number 0) balance the equation.
